Those are the questions which the lumbermen of northern Ontario want answered. Those are the things that industry wants to know, because those are the things that disorganize industry and make people feel that they cannot get the cooperation of this government that they should have. It is a serious situation, a serious indictment of the whole manpower policy of this government.
These boards are set up; very often they do things that are ridiculous. If we were not engaged in a war in which our very life js at stake, some of the regulations that are made, and unmade the next day, would be a joke. I sometimes think the minister says to himself, this, that or the other should be controlled; I will hunt up someone who can do it. Accordingly he hunts him up and gives him an office, a desk, a secretary and a brief case.

And a
carpet.

Sometimes a carpet, and a pretty nice desk. He sits there and says to himself, I am here to control something; I am going to start to control. Immediately he starts to issue orders to control this or that or to do this or the other thing. In a short time the control has to be taken off or changed or the order unmade.
Is there anything more ridiculous to-day than the regulation of bus traffic in this country? The trip limit is fifty miles. A man gets on a bus wanting to go fifty-five miles. He has to get off five miles from the terminus and perhaps hire a taxi for the rest of the way, as many do, while the bus goes on with an empty seat. If you wish to go from Toronto to Bradford you take the bus for fifty miles, get off at a hay field, take a waiting taxi that takes you the rest of the way, the bus going on with an empty seat. The termini now for bus trips are not town to town but cornfield to turnip patch. The thing is so ridiculous.
Then we have control of truck traffic. Firms had special trucks built to handle their particular commodity. There are many such in my district. These trucks are of no use whatever for general cartage. They can now travel only thirty-five miles; they used to travel one hundred or one hundred and fifty miles. How do they get around this control? Some of the trucks are actually taken off the road; the tires are depreciating; the truck is depreciating; it is just so much waste machinery in the country. At least the government should have let them carry on until these specialty trucks were worn out. But if they do not lie idle they will carry the commodity thirty-five miles to where another branch has been established; the goods are unloaded from one truck to another and carried the next thirty-five miles, and so on until they reach their destination. Think of the waste of man-power. The thing is ridiculous.
As a result of this sort of thing people are beginning to lose confidence. The government ask for confidence. How can people have confidence in view of such silly controls as that?

I am in the midst of it; I can see what is going on, and I do feel that to handle industry, agriculture or any other branch of our national economy, only the very best men one can find should be appointed. The other day the Prime Minister referred to the fact that we were criticizing the men who had been appointed to these positions and said, "But the members of the opposition asked us to do this." Certainly we did. At the beginning of the war, when we saw something of what was going on, when we saw the disorganized situation that existed, we urged the Prime Minister to go out and get the very best men he could find in every branch of industry to come in as advisers to the government and organize us for the war effort. But we did not ask him to have them come in and usurp the rights of parliament, as they are doing to-day.
These are just some of the things I wanted to bring before the house, realizing as I do that if we are to go out and sell this war effort, these controls and these restrictions to the people of our constituencies, the people of this country; if we are to build up confidence as we in this parliament are doing the very best we can to do, then the foolish things such as I have recited should be cleared up at once. Seriously I say that the time for any political face-saving has passed. It is up to us to build up a confidence in the minds of the people of this country. We have a tremendous effort to put forth. This may be the deciding year of the war. The extra food, extra munitions, extra equipment and so on that we can produce this year may be the deciding factor of the whole war. Let us go to work on it, and let the Prime Minister do as the other day he said he would. If it is true that some of these men do not fit into the job, let them go; clean up some of these things as they should be cleaned up. Then he will get the backing of every member of the opposition.

Hon. P. J. ARTHUR CARDIN (Richelieu-Vercheres) Mr. Speaker, being now a private member of the house I could listen with the greatest freedom of thought and mind to the speech delivered by the new leader (Mr. Graydon) of the newly baptized opposition party in the house. I do not hesitate for one moment in extending to him my heartiest congratulations, first of all upon having been given the honour of representing his party in the house as opposition leader and, second, upon his brilliant first speech in that capacity. The hon. member has many personal qualities, and I do not hesitate to say that he possesses both in mind and intellect the necessary qualifications to occupy an important place in the public life of this country. Whatever his views may be, he will always, I am sure, enjoy the respect of all hon. members, even though they do not agree with the sentiments or opinions he may express when speaking for himself and for the party to which he belongs. He has been in the house for a certain number of years, not very many compared with the time I have served here; but during those years he has made a great number of friends, and has been respected by members sitting on both sides of the house.
His presentation was good. I listened to him with careful attention, and with a somewhat more independent state of mind and spirit than I would have, had I been sitting on the treasury benches. He offered a good argument, and laid the foundations for a good conclusion, but, unfortunately, he did not arrive at a logical conclusion.
He made reference in strong, harsh terms to the fact that parliament was in need of rebuilding its reputation before the public, and of creating or developing better procedure than had been the practice for a certain number of years. I agree with him on that point. Even if we do better than others, no one can dispute that the parliament of Canada does not at present enjoy the confidence and respect it enjoyed in the past.
The hon. member referred to the changing of the rules of the house. He was quite right. Our rules of procedure are obsolete. They have been framed after the rules followed at Westminster, but here we have not developed the methods and customs prevailing at Westminster. There is an urgent necessity for a change in the rules of the house, a change in our methods of procedure.
But, even if they are obsolete, the rules of the house in many respects are not observed

The Address-Mr. Cardin
This is particularly true in connection with the reading of speeches. That is something which helps to discredit parliament. To a certain extent the chamber has become what we call in French-I do not know the English expression'-un cabinet de lecture.
It may be that under certain circumstances there is the necessity for reading a statement. However, I have lived long enough in political life to have seen great leaders of the past-Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden, Sir George Foster, and other great cabinet ministers- who were satisfied with only a few notes, even when making in the house a statement on the most important questions.
Exceptions may be made for the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, but this procedure of reading speeches should not prevail on every occasion and on all questions. Knowing the present Prime Minister as I do,
I can say that he is a master of the English language, a master of his own mind and of his own thoughts. He says exactly what he wants to say at any time and in all circumstances. He does not need to put down on paper five or six days or a week in advance what he wishes to say in the House of Commons. He has a great gift of learning, and to my mind he would be the last one, had the practice not been developed in the past few years, to ask to be allowed to read his speeches or statements on matters of secondary importance.
The reading of speeches has developed into a habit by all parties in this house for some years. The other day we listened to a very good speech delivered by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell). It was a very good speech indeed, but if he will allow me to say so he nearly spoiled it. Fortunately for him he is a good reader, and it was not too apparent that he was reading a text. But I would always prefer to hear the gentleman give his ideas as they occur to him while he is on his feet, his speeches are then far more effective.
There are many other aspects in which the rules should be amended. I have no time to go into them now. I shall make only a brief reference to Hansard. I do not know whether I would be in favour of abolishing Hansard. But few people read it now. In the old days it was referred to very often by the leaders of all parties with a view to discovering some contradiction of statements. Nowadays, however, we do not bother about contradictions. We have contradictions not only between what was said in past years and what is said to-day, but we have contradictions in the very same speech. The end of a speech does not agree with the beginning and very often the beginning contradicts the conclusion. Thus I
see no great need for recording what is said. Under the pretext Of new conditions and of changed times leaders contradict themselves and continue blithely their way on, not worrying at all about contradictions. They do not care whether the stand they took a month, or a week, or a day ago, agrees with their present attitude.
There are many other reasons why parliament is coming into public discredit and among then I might cite the positions which are taken by members or leaders in flagrant contradiction with their declarations to the electors. There is also the hesitancy shown on any question which might gain or lose votes to a party or group. In the end all these things come to the electors, first, causing them to doubt and finally casting discredit on parliament.
With all due deference, and with all the personal friendship I have for him, may I say to the leader of the opposition that his amendment to the main motion is an example of those hesitating moves and vacillating attitudes which help to discredit parliament in the eyes of the people. I cannot vote for the conclusion of his speech. I would have been ready to accept most of the premises that he laid down, but the conclusion of his argument as contained in the amendment that he moved to the address is not in accordance with the premises. The amendment is vague, as vague as it can be. It is obscure and lends itself to all kinds of interpretations. Any party or group in this house could find therein something that would accord with their views.
Unfortunately the same remark applies to the subamendment which has been moved by the distinguished leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. It is presented in general terms which need to be explained in detail and which for the most part are not clearly understandable for the man on the street. With all due respect to both hon. members, I will say that the amendments appear to have been drafted with the idea of gaining support from people of opposite views. It shows lack of courage to state precisely the policy proposed or suggested. The amendments which have been moved, the speeches which have been delivered and, I might add, with some hesitation, the attitude of the government remind me of a man trying to ride three horses at the same time, and trying to be Santa Claus offering something to each group in order to satisfy all shades of opinion. But that cannot be done very long without destroying the confidence of the people of Canada in our parliamentary institutions.
The Address-Mr. Cardin

Boards have been appointed, without any responsibility to parliament, to deal with matters which the departments could very well have taken care of. We have hired the services of outsiders who know nothing of politics and have had experience only in the limited field of their personal business activities. These boards are deciding public matters according to their whims. In their inexperience they are destroying established practices and customs which have been in existence in our country for over fifty years. The civil laws are being disregarded. The privileges and rights of the provinces are being interfered with by men who have no responsibility except the one of preparing a report to their minister. That is their only responsibility. Members of parliament have no importance and have no authority with these boards, these extraordinary men, these supermen who are directing the affairs of the country at the present time. In due time, all this comes to the ears [DOT]of the people and helps to discredit our administration. We are fighting for liberty, we are fighting for democracy and parliamentary institutions. Yet most of our activities are in the hands of little potentates, men of no experience, dictators in the field that has been given to them for administration. These new appointees are nominally dollar-a-year men, but they receive salaries from the organizations to which they belong. I do not suggest that they are doing anything wrong, but certainly they are not likely to do anything prejudicial to the firms with which they are connected. There were in the public service numbers of men who could have been brought together and could1 have administered and directed efficiently many of our war activities.
Propaganda is also a source of discredit to parliament. Propaganda such as is carried on to-day under such high-sounding titles as "winning the war" and "war service" is some kind of blackout of the intelligence of the population of Canada. The people are not getting the truth. Most of the time they are listening to appeals based on imagination, *sentiment, feelings and half-truths, all this calculated to arouse unfairly the emotions *of our people.
Something which happened not long ago is a flagrant breach of a promise solemnly made in this house and of record. We were handed a few days ago a document, "Canadian War *Orders and Regulations. Extra" dated February 1, 1943. It will be recalled that under the mobilization act of 1940, section 5, it is required that orders and regulations passed under the authority of that act, -when parliament is not in session, "shall forthwith be

published in the Canada Gazette'' and distributed to the members of the House of Commons. Well, that little document dated February' 1 carries on the first page an order in council dated January 19. It informs us that orders in council have already been passed on September 4, September 14, November 3, and December 8-orders in council based on the disposition of the mobilization act to send recruits outside Canada. The first order in council of September 4 andi the others were not printed or published in the Canada Gazette at that time. They lay dormant in the desk of the privy council from September 4 until January 19, or February 1. Is that observing the law and causing the printing of the order in council and its distribution "forthwith"? No; it is taking advantage, as I predicted would be done, of the last sentence of section 5, which provides for special circumstances.
The government took the power, when the amendment was passed, when Bill No. SO was adopted, to order that publicity should not be given to decisions of the government W'hen they felt it would not be in the public interest to 'do so. This is a breach of a promise. I remember very well the answer which I received on that point last session from' a member of the government, "Oh, do not fear that this clause is going to be taken advantage of; if the power is used it will be only under the most extraordinary circumstances. "We propose," said that gentleman, "to publish the orders in council and make all our actions public." That pledge has been broken. What danger was there to the national interest in making public on September 4 that we had sent recruits to Newfoundland? In what way could our war effort have been prejudiced by letting the public know that we had decided to use the recruits as regular volunteers and members of the militia of Canada? In no way could this have prejudiced our war effort or caused any difficulties, or have brought information of any real advantage to the enemy.
To-day we find that in orders in council the names of the regiments are omitted', because it is not in "the national interest" to say that regiment number three or regiment number five has been sent here or there. How can the disclosure of such a fact be destructive to our war effort? How can it give to the enemy encouragement or support or useful information to state that we have sent a certain regiment to replace another in Newfoundland? This gives the people an indication of what is going to happen if some day the government decides under the authority of the

mobilization act to send our sons and recruits overseas. These methods do not help to maintain the prestige of parliament.
The speech from the throne contains many words, but is rather poor in substance. As my time is running short I will be brief in the observations I shall make on the speech from the throne. There is the question of redistribution. That is nothing new. It has to be done in accordance with the constitution. But there are rumours that we shall not proceed with the bill. Newspapers have already stated that owing to certain difficulties, and to the fact that certain provinces will lose some seats in the house, the bill may be postponed until after an election. At any rate that is what I have read in the newspapers.
Parliamentary secretaries are to be appointed. That is not new either. I do not think this is necessary. My remarks are not to be taken as a reflection on the personality of those who have been chosen already and, as I am told, have already started their work. They may all be good men, deserving recognition and deserving to be trained in the business of the house. It is quite all right from that point of view, but to my mind it is the fifth wheel of the wagon.
Our position is not the same as in England where the government has to direct national and imperial affairs, together with what correspond to our provincial and municipal organizations. We are a small country and a small parliament, from the point of view of responsibilities, in comparison with the parliament of Great Britain, and this is an expenditure which we could easily avoid when our taxes are already high.
After all, what are the parliamentary secretaries going to do in the house? When they are asked a question about something that has been dealt with in the privy council they will be unable to answer, not being members of the cabinet. When they are asked a question on a matter of policy of the government they will not be in a position to- answer because they are not members of the government. In fact, they will be only glorified private secretaries or deputy ministers; that is all. On all questions of policy they will have to promise information for the next day, and the next day they will read a statement which will have been prepared by the minister or by somebody in the department. Well, such a statement could be read by any minister present in the house. It seems to me that our administration, with its numerous departments, its exceedingly large numbers of boards, commissions and controllers, is cumbersome enough without that additional machinery.
We have been told in the speech from the throne that national health will be taken care of and that social security will be looked after. But, as already mentioned by some other hon. members, these questions are largely provincial matters, and I hope we are not going to take advantage of the situation created by the war to deprive the provinces of the privileges and exclusive rights guaranteed them by the pact of confederation, without adopting some other satisfactory method which would protect minorities and guard the provinces against a central organization in Ottawa. With that limitation, what can we do? Very little. That is probably why the Prime Minister told us in his speech that these matters would be looked into, and probably that is all that will be done.
I question the merit of the study that we can make of the situation that will exist after the war. Where is the man bright enough and with vision enough, the man capable of prophecy, who is able to tell us what are to be the foundations upon which we shall build the welfare of Canada after the war? We shall find ourselves in a situation which none of us at the present time can properly envisage and determine. We may do a certain amount of work here and there, but it may very well be that when we are faced with the real situation after the war all the plans now prepared will be of no avail.
What is the use of building a house when we do not know upon what foundation it is to rest? Why lose our time in dealing with such uncertainties?
The speech from the throne also reviews our war effort. It has been a magnificent effort, I admit, and I am glad of it. All Canadians are proud of it, and we have the profound satisfaction of having it recognized that our war effort surpasses that of any other country of our size. As far as man-power and finance are concerned, our war effort is superior to that of the great republic to the south, the United States. Our war effort is really a great thing. It is abused, though, by a large number of people and is taken advantage of by many. Our war effort should be regulated by reason. There are certain problems which we must face courageously and one of the most important of these is agriculture.
I listened with great attention to the wonderful speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon, who always makes great speeches. He is a convincing speaker. Nevertheless the fact remains that there is a great man-power problem in the agricultural field in Canada. Whatever explanations may be given, even coloured with sentiment, they do not improve the situation.

Five minutes.
Is agriculture essential or not? It is essential. We ought to take every means to help this industry at the present time, because without it, without food products, however well-trained our men, however great our armament, the war would soon end. A man with an empty stomach is incapable of carrying the most perfect gun. Agriculture is the most important thing in the world at the present time. Canada, instead of trying to be first as far as man-power is concerned should strive to be first as far as agriculture is concerned, first in supplying food and armaments for the fighting

forces. There are countries capable of supplying more man-power than Canada. Russia and China have inexhaustible resources of manpower; there, men can be found in as great numbers as may be desired. They need the armaments and also the food we can produce.
Let us base our participation in the war upon reason; let us see that what we can do best is done first and not second, even if it is a source of pride for us that certain of our men are fighting gallantly at one point or another. We must sustain them, and we must, help to sustain Russia, China, and Britain and other parts of the British empire.
Munitions also are necessary, they are most important. The United States are thinking of fixing and limiting their man-power to 7,500,000 men. It is about time that we ourselves think of placing a limit-as high as possible, I admit-on our man-power overseas, and try to feed those who are in need of being fed. In north Africa people, are dying, and the political and military heads there to-day say that what has been provided up to the present in the form of arms and food is only a drop in the bucket and that unless something more is done in regard to food and armaments we shall not succeed and thousands upon thousands of the population will perish. The same situation prevails in China. China is threatened with famine, and she has not the armaments she needs to carry on her fight. Good old China, whom we love so much to-day, that we praise so much to-day and proclaim to be one of the first peoples in the world! For years she was fighting the Japanese on her own territory without our help, but to-day, what a change! We have discovered that she is a great country, a country that deserves our praise and support. We have modified our views; we have become a little more courageous and ready to help China now, as well as Russia. Let us give them what they need most, not men but food and armaments. That is what they want to enable them to carry on the struggle. As a matter of fact they are fighting for us as much as they are fighting for themselves.
If we have some success to-day, who has achieved that success? The Russians. Without Russia where would we be? Probably we would be signing a treaty of peace, not according to our terms or our will, but according to the will of others. That would be our position.
What are we to do? I am going to be bold, not afraid t-o express my thoughts. I regret that the government at the present time has not seen fit to suspend 'the mobilization act of 1940 until at least a survey has been made of the whole situation in order to ascertain the most pressing needs of Canada as well as of the united nations. We ought to make such

The Address-Mr. Cardin
a survey, instead of trying to attain the same end by a circular letter to be sent from time to time to the boards or to the committees that decide whether or not a man essential to the farm or to an industry should be given a military postponement. I hope we do not establish in this country, for coming generations, a practice by which those in authority are going to tell the judges and those who have been sworn to interpret the law what they ought to do and how they ought to interpret that law. I trust we have not reached' that depth. If the law is not good, let us change it, but while the law is there, let us observe it in the letter and in the spirit. What this letter purports to do is to tell the boards that they should interpret the law according to what the authority thinks it is important to do at a given time. If -that is what we are fighting for on the battlefield, we had better cease. If we are fighting for principles like those; if the law is to be changed according to the will of the government, according to the will of a superior officer, according to the will of a military authority, I do not know where it is going to end.
That is my suggestion, and I am not afraid to make it. I may be accused of not being alive to the situation, of not taking cognizance of the facts as they exist in the world to-day. To those who may be inclined to attack me and to be unjust I wish to say only this. To-day Irishmen are proud of Ireland even though their country is neutral. The Australian people are also proud of their country, though they have limited the extent of the field in which they are going to fight. They are still part of the British empire and of the British commonwealth. South Africa is still a member of the commonwealth and its people are still proud to be citizens of that country, although they have also limited the field of their activities in this war. The United States are looking after themselves and their interests first. They are helping to defend what we call liberty, democracy, etcetera; but I have not seen anything in the press nor have I heard a speech by any politician in that country stating that they were ready to give second place to their rights, principles, advantages and interests. Russia is fighting for herself, too. No public man to-day would deny that statement. Why can we not be Canadians, though participating in the war? Why do we not see our war effort through our Canadianism? In doing all we reasonably can to help win the war, we should not try to surpass, for vainglory or vain pride, the efforts of other countries who are more vitally and directly interested in the conflict than Canada?
One further word and I shall conclude. I have lived long enough to remember that one man, at one time very powerful in the United Kingdom and who was a close personal friend of our Prime Minister-I refer to the late Mr. Ramsay MacDonald-was not in full accord with the government of. his country in 1914-18. He was not in favour of England going into the war as deeply as she did in those years. Who would say that Ramsay MacDonald was not a good British citizen and a great man? A few years later he became Prime Minister of Great Britain, and we acclaimed him here in Canada when he paid us the honour of a visit. Perhaps that might answer those who may be inclined to criticize me too severely.
Something was mentioned about Casablanca. Either the leader of the official opposition or my good friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation asked the Prime Minister to make a statement with regard to the conference which took place between Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt in that city. Before six o'clock, that day, the Prime Minister began to give his explanation, brilliantly as always, with a fine choice of words and a careful weighing of his sentences and expressions. He presented a very good argument. After six o'clock he continued by reading a document he had prepared on the same subject. As the Ottawa Journal put it the next day, the statement before six o'clock was much better than the one after six o'clock.
The Prime Minister gave many reasons why Canada was not represented at that conference. The first was, "Well, I was not invited." That reminded me of a little story regarding a visit which Emperor Napoleon paid to a little town in France. He was received by the mayor of the locality who explained to him that for various reasons they could not fire a gun in his honour on his arrival. In fact the mayor said that he had fifteen reasons for not having fired a gun, and he proceeded to enumerate them: "First, we have no gun." Napoleon interrupted him and said, "Well, I do not want to hear about the other reasons; that suffices me." The moment the Prime Minister told us he had not been invited to the Casablanca conference I thought that was good enough, and that no other explanations were needed to indicate that while not invited he was there not in person, but in thought, and also through knowledge, because General McNaughton who is in close touch with the military authorities must have, in all probability, been aware of the questions discussed
The Address-Mr. Cardin

at the Casablanca conference. All these excuses and arguments were not as good as the first reason the Prime Minister gave before six o'clock, namely, that he was not invited.
1 am not humiliated because we were not invited. We had no reason to be there. We had no place there, because we are not one of the main powers conducting the war. Our authority is secondary; our role is second to that of many others, and we must accept the decisions of the powers mainly responsible for carrying this war to a successful conclusion. We had no reason to be there, and we have no reason to complain because we were not invited.
Let us adjust ourselves to our role, to our position. We are a dominion. We are a member of the British commonwealth of nations. But we are not as powerful as England; we are not as powerful as the United States; we are not as powerful as Russia. We are a small nation trying to do our best to help the sovereign nations and the great cause. We cannot hope to impose our will or our wishes when decisions as important as those which no doubt were made at Casablanca are to be reached. Let us avoid all unjustified pride of ourselves. We are in this war, it is true. We are in it to do the best we can. but as far as I am concerned, Canada comes first.
I am more interested in the welfare, wellbeing and maintenance of Canada than in anything else. It is all very well to coin phrases and to express opinions about this and that, opinions and coined phrases which in reality mean only one thing, that the end justifies the means. That is a nazi and fascist principle, and one to which I cannot subscribe.
We must be reasonable; we must keep our feet on the ground and not lose our heads in the clouds of excitement and exaggerated pride. Let us not exaggerate the importance and the extent of the contribution we can make in this struggle.
Let us be Canadians; let us think as Canadians and let us act as Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in coming to the conclusion that I should participate in this debate I was motivated by a very strong desire to give expression to my feelings regarding matters of current concern, and matters of future concern referred to in the speech from the throne. May I say at the outset that I cannot subscribe to the theory frequently advanced in the house that, through agreement or through some type of understanding, we should bring about a hasty conclusion to the debate on the address in

reply to the speech from the throne. After all, this is the occasion upon which the private member has an opportunity of dealing with those many matters which affect not only his constituency, 'but all of Canada.
Upon entering the new year Canadians were greatly encouraged by the improved military position of the united nations. I fancy that it is not an exaggeration to say that we have been inspired by the offensive action in North Africa-offensive on our side,, because we showed aggressiveness; and offensive so far as our enemies were concerned, because of the effect it had upon them. Furthermore, we have unbounded admiration for the people in the British isles who continue-to carry on not only the defence of their shores against a threatened invasion but also-the production of vast supplies of the tools of war and of the foodstuffs necessary to carry them through during the prosecution of the war.
We have been impressed, too, by the significant and heroic achievements of our Russian allies. All of those to whom I have referred are indeed deserving of our deepest gratitude. It would not be appropriate for me to proceed without further -asserting that we entered the new year full of admiration for and confidence in the men of our own fighting forces who have gone into theatres of war on our behalf.
There is one danger, however, with which we are confronted at the present time. I fancy that as a result of the fact that at least for the most part the battles are now extremely favourable to us, we may relax our vigilance and endeavour to -hide behind a cloak of optimism. We have among us too many volatile analysts and amateur strategists, if I may so describe them, who may endeavour to convince us that all is well, that the crisis is past, and that we may now relax. We have been told that the war will be long, that it will be bitter and bloody. I am satisfied that we should look upon the conflict in the light of the fact that it will still be longer, that it will still be much more bitter than it has been in the past, and that it will also be bloodier. We have heard it stated -that the-price of victory is blood, sweat and tears. We have not had a great deal of that yet, but let us not be unmindful of the fact that there shall be -much of it.
In the speech from the throne many words were directed to the post-war world. I do not -agree with those who assert that at this time we should not concentrate any of our efforts and o-ur energies upon consideration of and preparation for the post-war period. With regard to that part of the speech from

The Address-Mr. Shaw
the throne which refers to the post-war world, we find that the government intend to endeavour to provide freedom from fear and want. They intend, so they assert, to provide insurance against the inevitable consequences of major economic and social hazards. I may be unduly pessimistic-if I am, I am not alone-but I must say that I see in the expressions contained in the speech from the throne only pious platitudes. I cannot believe they are anything else. I fancy they were designed to be soothing; and I am indeed satisfied that much of it will prove to be meaningless.
As I have said, I do not care to be unduly pessimistic; but all we have to do is to look back over the last ten years, when there was every opportunity to do something about providing freedom from fear and want. Nevertheless in those years we did so little. I remember all the fine phrases and meaningless expressions of those days. Therefore, when I remember that the same individuals passed out for our consideration, mainly at election time, fancy phrases which once more crop up, I cannot be assured that they are not again being used for the same purpose. I trust-and I think I am expecting too much-that there shall be clarification of the expressions contained in the speech from the throne. I should hope that we may be given something concrete, so that our faith may be bolstered, so that we may be encouraged to exert ourselves to an even greater extent in our efforts to bring to fruition the promises now handed out so freely. Unfortunately, for decades politicians have been providing us with these vague phrases which, in almost every instance, have eventually proven that they could give us nothing but economic indigestion and disillusionment. Freedom from fear and want-I wonder what that means. I wonder which hon. member of this house can rise in his place to-night and tell us what he means by the expression "freedom from fear and want", and what he proposes to do in an effort to bring about that condition. We insist, Mr. Speaker, upon the government giving us something concrete and definite with regard to the post-war measures which they have in mind.
Another matter which comes to my mind is this:	Are our changes to be basic? Are we
going to get right down to business and endeavour to determine what these things are that have in the past caused the deplorable conditions which have been imposed upon us? Or are we going to devote our energies toward finding palliatives, patches, if you please, in an effort to make the old system perform functions which, deep down in our hearts, we know
it never can perform? I assert that there should be a commitment in this regard; I assert that if we are merely to have a few more schemes comparable with unemployment insurance, the government might just as well introduce their bill now and get the misery over with as soon as possible. It would be a waste not only of the time of this house but of the money of the Canadian people if the energies of the members of this house were to be centred upon the searching out and utilization of patches. We have had enough of that, Mr. Speaker.
Furthermore, when I try to determine to my own satisfaction just what faith I should have in the government when it comes to the laying down of a sound post-war economy, I reflect back upon some of the policies which have been so dear to them in the past. I shall refer to only one or two, and that only briefly.
First, the old age pension. I hesitate to mention that for fear I might incur the wrath of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), who, last year, when I made reference to old age pensions, chastized me because he asserted in effect that owing to my extreme youth I could not know anything about the conditions which prevailed among the old age pensioners.
I think the hon. member is wrong.

That is just my hon. friend's opinion.
If the government are sincere in what they contend they are going to do or at least try to do, they could at least take a step forward and show their sincerity by immediately increasing the amount of the old age pension and lowering the age qualification. I go one step further. I say it is criminal that when the son of an old age pensioner joins the active service forces, and assigns part of his pay and secures a dependent's allowance for his parents the old age pension should be reduced accordingly. I repeat, that is criminal, and I say that without qualification.
Then, with respect to veterans' pensions. We are continually receiving letters from veterans of the first great war-yes, and my hon. friend beside me says, from veterans of the Boer war too-letters from veterans who have suffered degradation as a consequence of the reward which they received from the government of this country after they had offered their lives in its defence, and who in many instances returned to Canada maimed or otherwise impaired in health. I am not fond of quoting these cases, but I will make just a passing reference to one particular case.
The Address-Mr. Shaw

It is that of a man who went overseas in the last war and fought in the mud and hell of Flanders' fields. He lost an eye and about 88 per cent of the vision in his other eye. Let me pause to ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would you part with an eye for? Or 88 per cent of the vision of the other eye? I dare say you would place a fancy price upon it. But what do we do about the other fellow? Here is this fellow given a pension of $20 a month. Then, because he took over a rural post office that pays him about $100 a year, less a ten per cent compulsory deduction for war savings, and because he raised $78 worth of grain and had one or two pigs to eat the slop, if I may use that term, the government officials came along, surveyed the situation and declared that his pension would be reduced by $10 a month. How can we expect a government that will condone actions of that sort to do anything for the boys who return from this war? Personally I cannot 'be led to believe that much can be expected. Mind you-alii hon. members know it, I do not have to tell them-the case I have cited is only one case out of scores and scores and hundreds. As an indication of our good faith let us wipe these cases off the books and, if it takes $100 a month to provide the necessities of life, let us say to these men: "We will give you $100 a month, and we will not send a government official to peek around the corner of your barn to see whether there are ten or eight little pigs in that new litter."
How about the men who are returning from overseas now? I have a placard; I have not it with me to-night but I carry it with me very frequently, which is about the size of this sheet I hold in my hand. It is divided into two sections. In one section it sets forth all the advantages that accrue to the boys who will don his majesty's uniform. It gives the rates of pay for the various ranks. Then it gives the dollar value of the hospitalization services, the medical services and the dental services which he may expect. All that is set out in detail. Then it shows the dependents' allowance and the separation allowance, and it is a glorious thing when it is all added up in a corner of the placard. It just makes the fellow wonder why the government told him a few years ago that they could not afford to pay him more than twenty cents a day in a relief camp. Then in the other section are listed the advantages that accrue to the man upon his discharge, and they look beautiful too, especially when nailed on the telephone poles on every corner of my town. But it is not what the government promise

that I am concerned about. What I am concerned about is what they do for the boys who are coming back now every day.
There is in my town a man who spent almost two and a half years overseas in this war. While on manoeuvres he was involved in an accident in an army lorry. His chest was crushed; his collar-bone was broken, and his arm was fractured. He came back to this country after being in hospital overseas for several months. He was discharged upon reaching this country. He appeared before a medical board and they assessed the damages which he had suffered. I might digress at this moment to give expression to my thoughts with respect to some of the boards, but I will try to curb my emotions at this time and refrain. This man, who cannot to-day carry on work, is receiving the noble sum of $7.50 a month; and he had to fight for that. The government cannot fool the people of my town, even though it used to be a Liberal town, when things like that are happening all the time. That means more than what appears on these papers. Let us show these boys that our statements are more than pious platitudes, more than surges of emotion that are here to-day and gone to-morrow. Let us prove through our actions that we are sincere in what we said about the things we are going to do for these boys who are fighting that our country may be preserved. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) tells me not to forget the girls who are in uniform too. What I say about the men applies also to the girls in the service.
What the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said this afternoon with respect to agriculture did not fool me one iota, nor did it cause me to change my notes a fraction. Black is black to me regardless of who may contend that it is otherwise. We live back in those constituencies; we know what those farmers are confronted with, and it does not take a Minister of Agriculture or anybody else to tell us what those conditions are. To-day agriculture in western Canada is in a wild state of confusion, and I find it difficult to imagine that after this war, when all available foodstuffs will be required to assist the people of the depressed countries, out of the confused agriculture of to-day there can then emerge a stabilized agriculture.
In my own constituency, of which I speak because it is the district with which I am most familiar, approximately sixty per cent of our threshing could not be done last fall. I am not minimizing the fact that we had an unusually bad fall, but at the same time I am not overlooking the fact that farmers in my constituency do not operate threshing rigs with

The Address-Mr. Shaw
two teams in place of six or eight just because they like to do so. Sixty per cent of our coarse grains and our wheat are either under the snow in the stooks or in swaths on the ground. The farmers in my constituency are mixed farmers, or, to use a more dignified expression, they carry on a diversified type of farming. They have encountered almost unbearable difficulties as a result of the acute shortage of feed for their live stock. I wish I could have the Minister of Agriculture in my constituency and take him for a drive.
Take him for a ride.

"Take him for a ride," my hon. friend says. I will refrain from commenting on that.
The day before I left my home town to come to Ottawa I met a certain lady. I did not go out searching for her; I had not known her before that day; but she was introduced to me as one who had encountered great difficulty on account of the shortage of man-power. This lady is forty-six years of age; she lives with her eighty year old mother on a thousand acre farm not far from the town of Innisfail. I do not say that all of the thousand acres are under cultivation, but a large part of the farm is cultivated. They have sixteen milk cows which they milk morning and night; they have 100 hogs, they have 200 sheep. Last fall, after they had put in their own crop in the spring, they were obliged to cut and stook it. Unfortunately they did not get it threshed. Shortly before I met this lady she had purchased 2,000 bushels of coarse grain for the hogs, and she had shovelled all of it herself, both on to the wagon and off it after it was hauled to her place. That is but one case; I did not search for a glaring example of what we are up against.
The man-power shortage is attributable to these facts. A very great number of young men from my constituency have joined the active service. As I stated before, I reside in a town of approximately 1.200 people, and from that town and the immediate vicinity 430 men have enlisted. On top of that, the government exercised the authority vested in them under the National Resources Mobilization Act and drafted a number of men. Speaking with respect to the draftees, and the difficulties which we have encountered in connection with our agricultural problem as a consequence, I should like to refer to the letter which the Minister of Agriculture read this afternoon. To me that is one more headache, for two reasons. First, there is still too much of an indefinite nature about that letter; and second, there should be a 72537-19
postscript, "Please read this when you get it. ' I am satisfied that many of the officials whom we have in the selective service offices are in a mild state of confusion-or probably it is not so mild-on account of the fact that the instructions they receive can be interpreted in so many ways, and because, in many instances, that hard-boiled officialdom has cropped up again. Talk about an instruction such as this:
Applications for leave should be invited from agricultural workers engaged in alternate work service, and such applications should be given favourable consideration.
To me that is bosh, in view of the experiences we have had. We have sent men to the selective service offices; we have begged for postponements because we knew definitely that they were urgently required, and we could not get them. There should be a clear-cut. definite and immediate investigation into the operation of the selective service offices. I got just beyond the point I wanted to cover, but these are the facts which I wished to place definitely and clearly before the house.
Unless our old age pension question is settled, and settled forthwith; unless we have these necessary revisions in the veterans' allowances and so forth, applicable to men of the last war as well as to those sent home during this war, and until such time as we have a clear-cut and definite man-power policy in this country, so that our agricultural industry will not flounder and ultimately fail- until we give consideration to these matters and thus prove our sincerity, we have no business talking about promises, the glowing promises of a grand, new posb-war order.
There is another matter about which I should like to speak, because I believe that in this regard we encountered difficulties in my part of the country far more serious than those in other parts. I refer to the acute fuel shortage during this winter. I fancy that some hon. members have read in the press that in the city of Red Deer we were burning our fences and so forth. Mr. Speaker, I propose to speak on a subject that is rather novel here, namely, the working of parliament, a subject that should interest us, because nothing is more interesting than the work we do.
Last session, on two or three occasions a number of hon. members referred to the working of parliament and made suggestions that something should be done to gear up parliament so as to make it a more effective instrument for helping the country and directing its efforts in the war. On May 26 last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) had this to say:
In my judgment parliament is more and more on trial at the bar of public opinion. There is something wrong with this House of Commons. I am not reflecting on the house, and I do not know what is the cause. But there is something wrong with it.
Since then, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has proposed that it is time that we change the rules of the house, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) doubted whether this was a suitable time to do so. Meanwhile hon. members and the people are making two sets of comments about parliament. One is that parliament just talks; the other is that parliament is a rubber stamp, that its members are not independent enough. I ask hon. members how they would like to have the house full of some of our most independent members. I will not name them, but let hon. members think of them for themselves. We must have parties in order to organize opinion, or we would have a totally different system from the one in which we want to work.
Some of the criticism about the House of Commons and its working is just misinformed, and some of it probably is on account of the fact that some people are disappointed be-
72537-19i
cause some supporters of the government did not turn upon the government and turn it out. Other comment on the working of parliament results from the feeling that there is room for improvement and that we can do something about it so as to make parliament the great forum of the nation and a better expression of the national will.
I would suggest-and here I think all hon. members will agree with me-that there is no more certain way of weakening parliament than to sneer at it and its workings. We can all try to improve it, but there is no point whatever in just saying, What is the good of it?
If there is one answer to be made to the criticisms so far made about parliament it is that nobody seems to have studied and expressed why it is defective, if it is defective; what can be done to change it, what should be done, and when. So far we have not had a debate on the subject, because there is no way under the rules to have a debate relating exclusively to this subject.
It is not my suggestion that the rules should be substantially altered. My view is that the rules are all right for the most part, but that changes should be made in the way in which we work the rules and that this will effect all the reforms that anyone would want to make. As I go along I propose to compare our procedure with the procedure in the British house. I do that for this reason, that the British people have had a very long experience of the workings of parliament, including a great deal of experience with the working of parliament in crises. Quite properly we regard the parliament at Westminster as the mother of parliaments, and the working of that parliament throughout the trials of this war has been one of the reasons why the whole world admires the British people. But I do not say that we should copy it in everything.
If time permitted, I should like to examine some of the rules of the congress in the United States and the parliaments of other members of the British commonwealth. I suggest that we can learn from the experience of other parliamentary bodies, and at the same time that we have a great deal in Canada that is better than is found anywhere else. But I do hope that hon. members will agree that if there is room for improvement we should try to make the improvement.
Please do not think I am setting up as an expert in parliamentary procedure. I recognize my own inexperience and limitations in that regard. It just happens that I have been interested in the subject, as other hon. members are; I have discussed it with older
The Address-Mr. Claxton

members and members of other parliaments whom I have known, and have read something about it.
The point at which I begin is this, that the rules, the procedure of parliament here and everywhere else were primarily designed for the passage of legislation. If one studies the matter and looks through the rules, one sees that they are designed to promote the enactment of legislation. Parliament is a legislative body; that was its primary function. But when we get into a state of war or meet the developments that have occurred in the last few years we find that the functions of parliament have changed. To-day parliament does not spend much of its time in enacting legislation, considering bills and passing them; it is the executive, the cabinet, which makes most of the laws, and of necessity it must be done in large measure by the executive. To-day the main function of parliament is to support and control the executive and to conduct a kind of government by discussion, so as to keep the executive continuously responsible through parliament to the people, and also to keep the executive efficient and give it every support that we can. My submission is that the practice we have continued to follow in Canada is the practice that is adapted for the purpose of passing legislation, while in Great Britain the parliament at Westminster, under exactly the same rules, has adapted a practice which is more suitable to the changed conditions of the times.
May I illustrate that. Since this debate commenced we have had some six or seven days discussion on the address; and as everyone knows, this is a general debate. Let me take just a single day, February 4, and look through the discussion that took place on that occasion. On that day different members spoke about food control, social security, women's war work, the officials of the wartime prices and trade board making speeches, nutrition, wooden ships, the Japanese in Canada, fuel shortage in British Columbia, food control, farm labour, social security, farm income, man-power, fuel shortage, reinforcements, redistribution, national income, pensions, post-war developments, production and employment, farm prices, post-war, food, farm prices, farm labour, social insurance, farm labour and labour. Similarly we could go through any general debate that occurs in the house, either this debate or the budget debate, and see subject after subject touched upon by one speaker and then perhaps left for three or four days before being taken up by another. That also has been illustrated to-night. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) who preceded

me did not follow the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), and as yet I have not followed either of those two hon gentlemen in their remarks.
The point I make is that in a general debate of this kind there is no possibility of having consecutive discussion relating to a specific point. I suggest that there are ways and means of having that. What I have just said about general debates of this kind is perhaps even better illustrated by what happens in connection with the war appropriation bills. It will be remembered that in 1940 we had a general debate on the war appropriation bills and the conduct of the war. Throughout that entire debate the members of the cabinet, almost without exception, were continually in their seats, wasting their time-which is more valuable than the time of anyone else in this house or this country

in listening to that discussion, a great part of which did not concern them. In 1941 we spent some thirty-six days in that debate, covering about 806 pages of Hansard, and I believe I mentioned once before that the then leader of the opposition had no less than 954 separate innings. At the same time in the British house they were voting ten times as much money by a similar though not the same procedure. The debate in the British house covered forty pages of their Hansard and was completed in three days. In closing the debate the chancellor of the exchequer made a speech consisting of five sentences, of which I will quote the last three:
I think only one direct question was put to me in the course of the debate. It was directed to ascertain my estimate of the revenue we expect during the coming year. I am sorry that I cannot give that information.
On the conclusion of that sentence he sat down, completing his answer to the discussion that had gone on. That was his only contribution to the debate, apart from his opening speech. Contrast that with the ordeal through which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) had to go, sitting here day after d>ay answering thousands of questions, then stepping right from the war appropriation bills into the budget debate and doing precisely the same thing.
In 1942, the session just concluded, the practice was extended of dividing up the debate and taking the service departments one at a time. I think all hon. members will agree that was a great step forward. All that I suggest is that this practice be carried two or three steps further forward. At the end of that debate in 1942, after we had spent twenty-nine days in a general discussion of the conduct of the war, the Minister of

The Address-Mr. Claxton
Finance made available a general break-down of the expenditures of a great number of departments, and for the last six days of the debate the discussion was related to that break-down. From that time on, the discussion was closely directed to the specific points set out therein, and we made very much better progress.
My suggestion is that in view of the tremendous burden which is placed upon the government and upon parliament, in view of the changed functions of government as a result of the wide extension of the whole realm of governmental activities, there is no way in which the deliberations of parliament can be carried on effectively unless they are organized and controlled. I suggest that the time has come when this house should direct the government to assume the responsibility of allocating time to debate, day by day, and indicating precisely what subjects will be discussed and how long will be spent on them. Such a practice requires no change in the rules of the house. It requires acquiescence on the part of members of the house; it requires that they should discipline themselves and cooperate with the government in seeing how best we can do the work of this house, to make it the most effective instrument for carrying out the national will. In Great Britain, again, that is actually done to-day. It has been done for a great number of years, and it is done under precisely the same rule that we have in Canada; namely, the order providing for closure. There is no provision in the British standing orders or rules for the allocation of time by the government. It is all done because the government has the power of closure if it desires to use it. Out of that comes the power of the government, acquiesced in by the other members, to arrange the time of the house; and of course in doing so the government consults with the Speaker and with the whips of the other parties.
I suggest that we might well look to the government and ask it to begin-not too rigorously at first-to proceed in this way when we come to the war appropriation bills which will come up for discussion within the next few days. In the United Kingdom they finished in December the debate on the address, corresponding to the debate now going on here. For that debate the government had allocated eleven days. Of those eleven days six were spent in general debate; five were devoted to private members' amendments, which is a very interesting development there. The total number of British Hansard pages devoted to the general debate was 185, and of the six days allocated to that debate the greater part of two were spent in secret session. But then, having finished the general debate in six
days, they went on to discuss a number of amendments which had been suggested by private members in order to concentrate discussion on specific points that were of general interest. Those amendments were selected by Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the various parties, as being the amendments which would concentrate the discussion on specific points, one at a time. I have in my hand copies of the British Hansard for the period I have mentioned, and when I come to No. 7 of the current session, for November 25, I see the first amendment that came up. It has to do with war injuries compensation. Then on the next day the next amendment came up, and they had a discussion on colonial development, a matter of great public concern in Great Britain and elsewhere throughout the world. Then on the third occasion they had a debate on reconstruction. That debate continued for two days, and during its course the paymaster general, Sir William Jowitt, who has charge of coordinating British work on reconstruction, made an extensive report to the house and to the country through the house, as to what was being done on that very important question.
If, however, the government is to have vested in it by the acquiescence of the house, or through the use or threat of closure, if necessary, the power to allocate the time of the house, and to designate specific subjects, then of course as a corollary the government must give opportunities for the discussion of subjects of general interest, and create such opportunities from time to time as occasion arises. In that connection I suggest that now there are one or two subjects of utmost importance to all of us, and with respect to which many of us would like to hear discussions, and would like to know what is happening. I refer first to the general international situation, and then to the particular development of defence arrangements in Canada, having regard to our very close and, I am glad to say, cordial and effective arrangements for the defence of this continent, in conjunction with the United States. Those are two subjects upon which the house should concentrate its attention for at least a day. I should hope very much that at some time in the future the government may be in a position to allow that.
In England, as we know, one of the most interesting, characteristic and distinguishing features of the British parliamentary system is the question period. Every day, according to the rules, from 2.45 to 3.45 p.m. there is a full sixty minutes of questioning. Questions are placed on the order paper the day before. Those for which oral answers are desired are
The Address-Mr. Claxton

marked with an asterisk. Each day from 150 to 200 questions are asked and answered. Very few of those questions are designed to get information. They are all designed to bring to the attention of the government a point of view or a grievance; and the form of the question is quite different from the form we follow.
I have chosen a question at random, and I find that it reads:
Sir W. Smithers asked the parliamentary secretary to the ministry of food what position Mr. Calder holds in his ministry; and what were Mr. Calder's connections with bacon factories previous to his appointment. . . .
Sir W. Smithers: Will the minister take steps to dissipate the idea . . .
And so on. The under-secretary makes reply. Then, the next question:
Mr. Thorne asked the parliamentary secretary to the ministry of food whether he will have some of the bread made of flour, oats and barley put in the tea room?
Not only have they questions, but supplementary questions are also allowed, within reasonable limits. As I say, very few of these questions are submitted for the purpose of getting information. They are designed to bring forward a point of view briefly and quickly, and that point of view registers for what it is worth. Often when this is done it obviates the necessity of putting the point in a more formal way in debate in the house.
Supplementing questions is the adjournment debate. It is quite a different matter from our procedure to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. The parliament at Westminster has that procedure, too. However, we have not anything like the debate on the adjournment. This is a procedure whereby, any member who is dissatisfied with the reply of a minister says, "I give notice that I will raise that on the adjournment," or else he gives notice without having a question. Then, the government may occasionally raise a debate on the adjournment. The whips get together and arrange that within a day or two when the normal time for the adjournment of the house takes place, opportunity will be given for a member to state his case. Two or three members may join in, if there is time, and the minister or under-secretary will reply, the matter thereby being disposed of when it is hot, and when there is still interest in it. That is the last that is heard about it. However, it has the result of releasing the subject at once, ventilating it and securing the attention of parliament, the country, and the minister. It also supplements the very effective method of interrogating the government by way of questions.

Almost every day there are adjournment debates. Even during the period I have mentioned, at the beginning of the last session of the house when the debate on the address was in progress they had, on the second day, a debate on estate duties; on the third day a debate on the situation and status of Prince Paul and Princess Olga of Yugoslavia; on the fourth day a general debate on the business of the house; on the seventh day a debate on Royal Observer Corps centres; on the eighth day a debate on essential work order; on the ninth day' a debate on the weaving mill at Tayport; on the tenth day a debate on a Royal Air Force, airmen's application; and on the eleventh day a debate on civil service pensions.
That is in the period of the debate on the address. Almost every day opportunity is given toward the end of the sitting for about a half hour to be spent in the ventilation of some subject. Through those devices of questions and adjournment debates it is possible for private members to bring matters to the attention of the government and the people exceedingly quickly. All my conversations with members of parliament at Westminster have indicated that they regard the question period as the most important single feature in British parliamentary institutions. As we all know, we have not that kind of question period here. Our practice is to ask questions which seek information, a great deal of which is sometimes available in blue books. Such information is placed on Hansard or supplied through sessional papers as orders for returns. I think hon. members will agree with me, however, that a great part of the material asked for in our questions is of no permanent value, and might just as well be obtained by the member through direct communication with the department or the minister. With respect to these other types of questions, may I point out that a very large percentage of them are of a contentious and argumentative nature, and have the effect of stating a case.
In addition, arrangements are made in the British House of Commons for the holding of debates on special topics. During the debate on the budget, for example, it may be agreed that the second day will be spent on some specific topic, and the third day on another. In that way they break down the whole broad scope of a debate into topics which can be handled. Members may speak consecutively, and ministers or under-secretaries may reply. In those debates there is a meeting of minds and a clash of wills. At once they become much more lively and interesting, and at once there is something the people can follow. At the same time it is a debate about which the

The Address-Mr. Claxton
press gallery can write, with interest. It is something which can be handled and which has some meaning, because it is not scattered throughout a whole session. For instance, statements respecting reconstruction, and thoughts in line with that subject, will be recorded' on one occasion. Having taken place on such an occasion they are not so likely to take place at other times. I suggest that in this way the parliament at Westminster not only secures more orderly and organized discussions, but saves the time of the ministers, who know when subjects are to be considered. At times when matters outside their interest are not under consideration, they need not be present.
Then, too, there is much more satisfaction in dealing with a subject in a manner which makes one feel that he is making some contribution, progressively. One idea, of course, leads to another. There is all the great advantage of discussion in a deliberative assembly, without the disadvantage of having a series of set speeches on different subjects, such as we are making to-night, and such as we make on other occasions when we have general debates.
We are told, of course, that the kind of thing to which I have referred should take place on the estimates. That may be so, and it may not. It depends upon the year. In 1940, the business of the house was such that we dealt on a very hot August day and night with 493 items in the estimates, totalling $191,623,349.69; that was on the second last day of the session, on August 6. In 1942, on the last day of the session, we dealt with 190 items totalling $251,974,758
