with; they were just voted.

They were voted, and
some of them were discussed. That was the only opportunity accorded for discussing the subject I am now discussing, the procedure in the House of Commons, because the appropriation for the House of Commons came up on that day. It is for that reason that I venture to take up the time of the house on this subject to-night, because on account of pressure of work another opportunity may not occur until very late in the session, and we know what it is to bring up a new subject in the house toward the end of the session. It would be like a little boy in class at school who does not understand a question, and who is scared to ask because he is afraid of getting the whole class kept in to hear the answer.
There are other suggestions that might be made in connection with the business of the house, but I would present for the consideration of hon. members in the government the suggestions I have made, namely, that time should be allotted to specific subjects; that they should be picked out and dealt with one at a time; that the question period should be extended and liberalized a little so that occasionally the government might commit itself on a question of future policy; that there should be adjournment debates and that debates, like the budget debate, for instance, might be divided up to provide an opportunity for the discussion of special topics. These proposals I have made could be carried out without a single change in the rules of the house. All they require is the general will of the membership of the house to put them into effect and the willingness of the government to carry them out, and I would hope that the government would be willing to do so because I can see no other way of saving the time of the government and making its work in the house easier than by means of these suggestions.
One further suggestion is in connection with committees. I think most hon. members would like to see the practice of referring matters to committees extended. I have had a very short experience in the house, only three years, but during that time I have served on some thirteen committees of which ten were active. During that time-and I know this is the experience of other hon. members-in no one of these committees was there a single vote on party lines. As soon as the members got on the committee they began to work seriously and intensely to find the best solution for the problem committed to them. If the problem was one which was suitable for study by a committee, and the committee was not too large, it invariably brought in a sensible, constructive report which was carried out by the government in every case except one.
I mention the size of a committee because it is my experience both outside the house and in, and the experience, I think, of other members, that the effectiveness of a committee decreases geometrically in proportion to the increase in its membership over fifteen. I think fifteen is the right number. It is the number fixed in the rules of the house. With a small committee of that size the members are much more conscientious; the responsibility is not diffused, and there is a much more steady attendance, a much closer discussion, and more opportunity for the members to meet in between meetings and work up material. Therefore I suggest that fifteen should be the maximum number for a committee, and I hope that this suggestion will be taken into consideration by the government when it comes to appointing a committee on social legislation.
The Address-Mr. Claxton

I think it is our experience that the chairman of a committee should preferably, not be a member of the government. I have sat on committees with chairmen who were members of the government, and I must say they presided magnificently. Nobody could have presided better or with greater objectivity, but at least on oDe occasion it led to some embarrassment that a member of the government should have been chairman of the committee. My idea in this is that once we get a matter out of the house and before a committee we lose the atmosphere of the arena and we get into the atmosphere of the workshop, where we want to do the job as quickly, effectively and efficiently as possible. That is my experience.
I suggest that some committees need expert assistance, and I sincerely hope that the committee on social legislation is not set up without a great deal of expert assistance, similar in standing, if possible, to that provided for the royal commissions in England which ultimately resulted in the Beveridge report. It is impossible for members of a committee to give the detailed work and study and have the background and special knowledge necessary to handle a topic of that kind.
Then the committee produces a report. By that time the matter has been screened through the committee, and the discussion of its report in the house provides an opportunity for a useful short dfebate on the subject, in which debate usually only the members of the committee take part. It has been my experience in the last three years that these debates have been the best in the house, and I do not think any one of them has ever taken more than a day.
We all know, too, that the mere fact that a committee may look into a matter has a salutary effect upon some government departments. I believe that in time we ought to have committees of the house on different subjects to which matters would be automatically referred, such as man-power and labour, munitions and supply, agriculture, reconstruction, international affairs and information-topics like that, and not merely matters which are to be the subject of legislation.
This brings me to my next suggestion. We have heard a great deal said about government by order in council, but the people who talk against government by order in council seldom say how government should be carried on. The fact is that we have the executive taking the responsibility of using the authority we have given to it, but the people who complain of government by order in
[Mr- Claxton.]
council would be the first to complain if the executive failed to use that authority. It is greatly to the credit of the government, parliament and the country that at no stage has our government failed to have the courage to use the authority it has been given. It alone of all democracies was the first to introduce effective measures to deal with the spectre of inflation. I see no other means whereby that could have been dealt with so effectively as by order in council. But we have had 25,000 orders in council, and now there is a kind of public clamour growing up against government by order in council which will grow as victory comes closer and people want to get rid of bureaucratic control, as they call it. To prevent this from growing to the point where it interferes with the conduct of the war and to preserve the supremacy of parliament, we must have some say at some stage in these orders in council, and in a great number of instances we cannot have it before. The practice of tabling orders in council is, for all practical purposes, an empty form. I suggest that orders in council be referred to a committee for consideration -not all the orders, 'but orders having the effect of legislation of a general nature. Even when they get to the committee, all the orders of that kind would not be discussed; but if the committee felt that one particular matter should be discussed it could take up that order, have the departmental officials there to explain it, and make its report to the house. This could be done exceedingly quickly. In this way there would be an opportunity of improving the drafting of the orders, which sometimes leaves a great deal to be desired; there would be exercise of control over tha executive, opportunity for ventilating grievances, and also observance of the important principle of the supremacy of parliament. I suggest that is one way in which it could be done without any sacrifice of the speed and decisive action which are necessary in order to carry on the war.
There is some need of an appeal from orders of 'a punitive nature. I do not see why all the boards which have orders of that kind should not act like the wartime prices and trade board; that is, use the courts exclusively. But in other cases anyone who regards himself as aggrieved by the application of an order in his individual case should have an opportunity of appealing to some authority other than the men who made, enforced, policed and executed the order. Therefore I suggest there should be an administrative tribunal of the same character as the war contracts depreciation board [DOT] or the board

The Address-Mr. Graham
appointed under the Excess Profits Act. Both of these boards have done magnificent work.
There also ought to be an appeal from all orders under the national mobilization regulations. It is the only way in whioh uniformity throughout the country can be preserved. It is the only way in which possible injustices through the board being too rushed can be corrected or further consideration given. Accordingly I suggest that there should be an appeal from all these boards to some authority.
In conclusion, I have this to say. We live at a time much more important in the history of parliament and of our country than any other. There is no one who should occupy a more important role in the life of Canada than the members of this house. Not only do people look to us for leadership and guidance; they want everything that we can give in the way of devoted service to our country. We are willing to give it, and I believe, from what I have seen of them, the members of this house of all parties would be only too anxious that their very real sacrifices of time, health, family life, and future expectations of a financial nature should be made more valuable to the country, and that I suggest, might come about through the further consideration of some of the suggestions I have made this evening.

A number of very fine addresses have been made in this particular debate. The speaker who just preceded me made an interesting contribution on an unusual subject, one which, of course, will have to be given great study, as he no doubt expected it would, before it can be accepted in its entirety. Nevertheless I should like to compliment the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) upon being sufficiently fresh in his viewpoint to introduce the subject and deal with it as he has done, indicating the considerable amount of study he must have given to the subject with which he dealt.
In addition, I wish to join those who have spoken before me in commending the addresses of the mover (Mr. Harris) and the seconder (Mr. Halle) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is for me a happy thought that I have in my constituency a highly thought of citizen who is a lady cousin of the mover of the address. I have a sense of pride in the fact that there is at least some connection between the far-off constituency of Swift Current and that of my hon. friend who moved the address in reply. My remarks of commendation of course apply equally to the hon. and gallant member who seconded the motion.
May I also say, and I think the house will agree, that it would be well to note the value of the address delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon. Regardless of our political viewpoints we, as a former speaker pointed out, are the representatives of the different sections which go to make up Canada; and the concise and cogent information given to this house this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture makes the task of every member that much easier.
May I also, in commenting upon the addresses in this debate, pay a word of compliment to at least two members of his majesty's loyal opposition. I refer to the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). The one dealt with agriculture, and the other with the industrial war effort of Canada. While I do not find myself in agreement with many of the points which they made, it struck me that they were moved by a sincere desire to criticize fairly and constructively the policy of the government with regard to these two important phases of our war effort. Constructive criticism, as rye all know, is a valuable adjunct of any government charged with the responsibiliy of carrying on the business of a nation.
The speech from the throne dealt with many matters of importance. The most important, of course, is the successful prosecution of the war. Anyone who read that speech or heard it at the opening of this session must have been struck with the fact that not only did it specifically express a note of confidence in our present position, as regards the war situation generally, but the very fact that the speech contained matters such as post-war reconstruction and social security indicates that there is in the minds of those who advised his majesty in the drafting of that speech a certain measure of confidence which will be heartening not only to the members of this house but also to the people of this country.
It is easy, too, to realize the truth of the statement that we can take pride in the progress which has been made in the successful prosecution of this war. It is only necessary to think back to the perilous days of Dunkirk, and to the time when we sat in this house and received the news of the fall of France, and compare the situation then with what it is to-day, to realize that progress has been real and substantial, and we can take pride in the immense advance which has been made upon the road to victory.

The -Address-Mr. Graham

Canada's war effort is becoming more and more a matter of great pride to all Canadians. That war effort is not the result of accident; it is of course the result of a sustained and well planned programme of contribution to the common cause of the united nations. I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government who have led the country in that effort can be justly credited with a great deal in so far succeeding as they have done in making Canada's contribution something of which we can all be proud. Not only that, but I say to members on this side of the house that those of us who saw fit to support the Prime Minister in the rather trying days of last session and the session before can all take a great deal of pride in recognizing that his aims and objects were dictated1 by wisdom, and in giving him that loyal support which enabled him to put that programme into effect.
I agree, however, with the note of caution expressed by the Prime Minister when speaking in this debate, that the measure of success which we have realized is only a warning to us of the path we must follow in order to achieve victory. We, in a democracy, of course hate war so intensely, and it is so foreign to our whole philosophy of Life to believe that other peoples would use war as an instrument of aggrandizement, that we welcome any sign of approaching victory and the time when we can turn back to the peaceful pursuits that so suit our philosophy of life. Yet we would1 be foolish indeed if we did not recognize the immense task that lies ahead of us. I read in a National magazine recently of the forces that Japan still has at its disposal to fight the battle in which we are engaged with that country at the present time, and they are still a great menace. She occupies vast territories that have so widened her economy that she faces want in one or two items only. She is immensely strong in man-power, immensely strong in ships, immensely strong in the strategic position she succeeded in securing for herself by her treacherous attack prior to the outbreak of war between herself and the United States. We must recall, too, that Germany is still mighty in her military strength, the accumulation of many generations of that race that seems so far to have been bent on world domination. As Germany is forced back on her own central home front, she solves many of her communication problems, and this leaves her with a freedom of action in defence, which we must overcome before victory can be ours. So that never for a moment, either in our hearts or in our minds, should we permit the feeling of optimism, or of con-

fidence even that pervades Canada at the present time, to weaken us in any way in the determination to see to it that Canada's material, physical and human resources shall continue to be used for the purpose we have before us, which is to defeat those forces of evil that so violently and disgracefully attacked the democracies.
May I also point this out. I think it is something we should note, those of us who by the nature of our position take a great interest in the political life, not only of this country, but of other countries as well, that in the commencement of the fourth year of the war the great democracies, Great Britain, the United States, Canada and the other component parts of the British commonwealth of nations, can feel that democracy, with all its apparent faults, has stood the test in the hour of trial, and that democracy is the democracy we have always known-a democracy of free parliaments, a free press, freedom of worship, freedom of speech, freedom in the expression of the opinons we see fit to utter so long as they do not offend the rights of our fellow men. It is a great thing to keep that in mind when discussing the relative merits of this or that kind of governing system. In the last analysis, these free democracies are standing the test, and we are all of the profound belief at this moment that ultimately they will achieve victory over the totalitarian states.
In passing, I would call the attention of those who advocate a planned economy, or the setting up of government whose control is vested in a group of experts to deal with the lives and the welfare of our people, to the importance of always keeping in mind that, despite the fact that Hitler has had many men of brains and capacity, sometimes regarded as supermen in Germany, and having devoted all the talents of that country to the planning of success in this war venture of his for world domination, nevertheless he and all his cohorts and experts will fail in the task to which they have set themselves. The same is true of Mussolini and Italy. So that I think the nature of the progress we have made should strengthen our belief in democracy as we have known it, and we should not hastily or lightly cast aside a system that has brought us the results it has during this war period.
It is true that our democracy has certain weaknesses. It is inclined to be hesitant in coming to a decision; it is inclined to engage in controversy to too great an extent; it is inclined to an inability to gird up its loins to exert its maximum war effort. Yet these weaknesses are the corollary of free institutions, and I am not afraid to say that the expression of these weaknesses in war time will become

The Address-Mr. Graham
the very strength and bulwark of the free institutions of democracy in the times which we so much desire that lie ahead.
There were one or two matters that arose either in the speech from the throne or during the discussions in this house of peculiar interest to me as coming from Saskatchewan. One was the suggestion, in fact the declaration of intention, that a redistribution of seats in this house should occur at this particular session. I add my voice to those from western Canada who suggest to the government that it would be extremely unfair at this time in Canada's history to propose that Saskatchewan, the third largest province in the dominion in point of population, and its neighbouring province of Manitoba, should find, largely as a result of the war effort and the transfer of people from the prairies to the industrialized sections of Canada, that they are penalized for making that contribution by losing, for a period of at least ten years, the number of representatives they have heretofore had in the house of commons. I am sure hon. members will agree that no other part of Canada has the troubles which have beset western Canada, struggling to construct an economy that will support itself, or deserves more the fullest measure of sympathy in this house which can be given it. I therefore strongly urge on the government and the members of this house, who in the last analysis will have the decision in the matter, that they exercise generosity in recognizing the cause of the shifting population from Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and that in any redistribution measure which may be introduced, the effect of that legislation will be deferred until 1953, or for a considerable period after the cessation of the war, so that we can then see whether the movement from those provinces has been temporary or permanent.
There is also the other matter that is constantly raised, without any fruitful results, I am sorry to say, namely, the concentration of Canada's industrial life in the two central provinces. I for one have always recognized and forgiven, if that is the proper word, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), having regard to the immense task with which he was presented during the early period of the war, in procuring the great amount of material that was required at once for Canada at war. I did not blame him much, that, on account of the necessity with which we were faced, in the early days of the war he seized upon plants that were already in existence and transformed them into the arsenals of munitions and supply that we so urgently required. Since then, however, there has been a great change. We have had time, and we have time at present, to consider the larger
question, the result of the great concentration of industrial activity in the central provinces and the failure of Canada as a whole to remove one of the constant points of irritation in confederation, and to see to it that decentralization takes place where it is wise and proper, and in that way balance the economy of the outlying portions of Canada to a greater extent than has been done hitherto. I believe that if we continue now on the path we have been following we shall continue on it in peace time as well. The fact that the plant, equipment, management and all the essentials are there will be used to justify the continuance of the use of those properties.
Hon. members know as well as I do that we have been seeking ways to use our surplus of wheat. I was told by one who ought to know that the United States government is spending immense sums of money and employing a large group of highly trained people to look into ways and means of using cereal crops for the manufacture of industrial products. For industrial alcohol, synthetic rubber and similar products we have in western Canada not only immense quantities of materials but immense potential capacity to produce those materials. We would thus be serving the best interests of western Canada and, indeed, of the whole of Canada if we could, to some extent at least, break up this concentration of industrial life in the two central provinces, which concentration sooner or later will cause serious trouble. We can do it wisely, and the whole of Canada will profit.
In listening to the different problems that were brought to the attention of the house during this debate, I naturally followed with great interest the speech delivered by the new leader of the official opposition (Mr. Graydon). I join with others in congratulating the Progressive Conservative party upon the choice of him as their acting house leader. I did, however, note that in putting upon Hansard most of the party's platform adopted at Winnipeg he did not include in the apparently important sections of that programme the resolution which the hon. member for-Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) succeeded in having passed at that convention and which had to do with the price of wheat. I am afraid that this was a child whose desirability was questioned at that convention.

I for one will welcome to my side at least and to the side of a great many hon. members on this side of the house any support that hon. members can give to that wise and beneficent policy that we have so long advocated.
Also I could not help noticing that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, suggested that the speech from the throne was merely a series of pious platitudes. He will not mind if I say to him that I listened with considerable interest to his radio address a couple of weeks ago and noted the fine manner of its delivery to the public of Canada. Nevertheless let me say to him that his address dealt only with generalities. The comment of a friend of mine next morning who said he had listened to the hon. member's address was that he had come to the conclusion that there were not many Canadian soldiers in Libya. I asked him why. He said, "Well, because if there had been Mr. Coldwell would undoubtedly have promised them ice and air conditioning". There xs an element of truth in that statement.
I have listened to thousands of expressions of opinion as to what should be done in this country, and almost without exception what one gets is a statement of a problem, phrased in varying language but still simply a statement of the problem; seldom is there any concrete suggestion as to how a solution of the problem can be achieved. The only time in his speech in this debate that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar became specific

Parliament does not give up its trusteeship when it votes money for the carrying on of the war.

As I say, to me the suggestion to which I have referred is a denial of the democracy I took the time to praise a few moments ago. As the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) said the other

Labour Conditions
night, it would mean the securing of social security at the cost of our individual liberty, to which I think no sane member of this house would agree. May I say, too, in all fairness to the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party that considering the task with which this country will be faced after the war is over; considering that some eight hundred thousand men will be coming back to our shores-at least we hope so-whom we shall have to place back in civil life in a reasonably prosperous condition; considering the dislocation that will occur in our industrial life, our farming life and, in fact, every phase of Canadian life as a result of this prolonged struggle, would any sane person suggest that in addition at this moment, or between novv and the cessation of war, we should agree to revolutionize suddenly the whole system of democratic government under which we have lived and under which we shall succeed in winning this war? Would anyone suggest that in addition to the problems which we shall have to face then, we should add the further problem of the dislocation that would result from any such change, even if that change were meritorious and justified?
Certainly we shall have dislocation if we do nothing.

I suggest that democracy can undertake the task of building upon what we have learned in the past, using the wisdom we may acquire during this war, to see to it that our problems are wisely met and our difficulties minimized to the greatest possible extent during the period of dislocation, reestablishment and reconstruction through which we must pass.
I now turn to the subject that really caused me to take part in this debate, one in which I take a great interest. I refer to the question of social security. As I have already stated, most of the contributions offered so far in the editorial columns of the newspapers and in speeches from different individuals have consisted of statements of the problem itself, statements of what we must face. Seldom is there any concrete, wise suggestion offered as to how social security may be achieved. Together with a great many members of this house I was very much interested in the fact that in England a commission headed by Sir William Beveridge, an economist of whom I happen to be a great admirer, brought forth what is now known as the Beveridge report, which, of course, as he has stated is only a suggestion for a solution of a certain phase of the social security problem. At least it is a concrete contribution, and I for one have greatly appreciated the opportunity of reading the result of the work of Sir William Beveridge and those associated with him in that task. Naturally his report applies peculiarly to industrialized Great Britain. I believe it is founded upon Liberal principles, according to my understanding of Liberalism. I believe members of this house and the people of this country would be well repaid if they carefully studied that report in order to ascertain the value of any ideas therein contained which might be beneficially applied in this dominion. However, I think I should say this, in connection with the whole programme for social security, that in our desire to bring about that result we must not assume that it will come simply because we are united in that desire.
